Titan Industrial Equipment - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Titan Industrial Equipment Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you will need to press star one on your telephone keypad. There may be a brief pause while we poll for questions. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Johnson, VP of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson (VP of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Titan Industrial Equipment's results for the Q3 2024. Joining me on today's call are Mike Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; and Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Mike Reynolds.

Mike Reynolds (CEO):
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on Titan Industrial Equipment's performance for the Q3 2024. We've made significant progress on several fronts, and I'd like to highlight a few key achievements. Order intake remained robust across our key end markets like construction, mining, and agriculture, with book-to-bill ratios staying well above 1x and backlog visibility providing strong revenue conviction. We've also seen meaningful compression in lead times for our core products and components, reflecting supply chain resilience amid ongoing global disruptions. Demand trends in construction, mining, agriculture, and manufacturing continue to show resilience, supported by infrastructure spending, commodity cycles, and reshoring tailwinds. These factors underpin our confidence in the key assumptions for our full-year guidance, including moderate economic growth and sustained end-market demand.

We are confident that our strategic initiatives are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa Chen to provide more detail on our financial results.

Lisa Chen (CFO):
Thank you, Mike. Turning to our financial performance, Titan Industrial Equipment reported $1.42 billion in revenue for the quarter, representing a 12% increase year-over-year. Gross margin was 39.2%, driven by favorable product mix, pricing discipline, and operational efficiencies in our Peoria and Monterrey facilities. Operating expenses were $285 million, resulting in an operating income of $320 million. Our net income for the quarter was $240 million, or $1.85 per share.

We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet, with $1.8 billion in cash and cash equivalents. We are committed to investing in our business to drive future growth and shareholder value.

Good morning, everyone. As we dive into the details, I'd like to focus on our order intake and book-to-bill dynamics, which remain a strong leading indicator for our Manufacturing and Industrial Equipment portfolio. Overall, Q3 order intake came in at $2.95 billion, up 14% year-over-year and 10% sequentially from Q2. This marks our seventh consecutive quarter of double-digit YoY growth, driven by robust demand across key end markets and our continued execution on capacity ramp-ups at facilities in Peoria and Monterrey.

Our consolidated book-to-bill ratio stood at 1.20x for the quarter—comfortably above 1x for the 11th straight quarter—reflecting a growing backlog now at a record $14.5 billion, up 24% YoY. This positions us exceptionally well for revenue visibility into FY25 and beyond, with approximately 68% of expected full-year revenues already in backlog. Let me break this down by end market, where we've seen differentiated performance tied to macro tailwinds, our product mix, and targeted commercial initiatives.

Construction remains our largest segment, with Q3 order intake of $1.25 billion, surging 20% YoY and 13% sequentially. Book-to-bill here expanded to 1.28x, fueled by infrastructure megatrends globally. In North America, orders for our next-gen hydraulic excavators—like the 350-ton Cat 395F model with enhanced fuel efficiency and telematics integration—jumped 27% YoY, supported by the IIJA's $550 billion spend pipeline. We're seeing particular strength in data center-related site prep, where wheel loaders and dozers accounted for 32% of intake.

Regionally, EMEA contributed 30% of construction orders, up from 24% last year, thanks to EU Green Deal-funded rail and highway projects. Asia-Pacific softened slightly amid China's property sector headwinds, though we're offsetting this with market share gains in India via localized manufacturing of compact track loaders. Strategically, we've launched our 'ConstructSmart' digital platform, integrating IoT sensors for real-time fleet optimization, which has driven a 17% attach rate on new orders—boosting aftermarket pull-through potential by 22-27% over the equipment lifecycle.

Mining orders hit $840 million in Q3, up a stellar 24% YoY and 16% sequentially, with book-to-bill at 1.35x—the highest in our portfolio. This reflects copper and lithium supercycles, with commodity prices up 17-22% YTD supporting capex cycles at majors like BHP and Rio Tinto. Our ultra-class haul trucks, such as the 797F with autonomous hauling capabilities, represented 42% of intake, as customers prioritize battery-electric transitions—our first BEV demo fleet in Nevada has secured $160 million in follow-on orders.

Latin America drove 37% of mining intake, led by Peruvian copper expansions, while Australian iron ore projects added another 27%. North America was up modestly QoQ after temporary permitting delays eased in Nevada lithium sites, with our backlog here growing 32% YoY. A key initiative is our 'MineOptix' AI-driven predictive maintenance suite, now standard on 72% of new rigs, reducing unplanned downtime by 20% in pilots and enhancing our sticky service contracts, which now comprise 47% of mining aftermarket revenues.

Ag orders reached $530 million, growing 11% YoY despite a slight sequential dip amid seasonal planting cycles and softening grain prices. Book-to-bill held steady at 1.12x, with backlog up 14% YoY to $2.2 billion. Precision ag demand is the bright spot: high-horsepower tractors like our 8R series with autonomous guidance systems saw 18% YoY intake growth, capturing share from John Deere in the U.S. Corn Belt.

North America accounted for 57% of ag orders, buoyed by farm income at $185 billion despite lower commodity prices, while Brazil's soy harvest expansions lifted LatAm to 22% of intake. EMEA faced headwinds from Ukraine-related fertilizer costs, muting orders by 6% YoY. We're countering with our 'AgriYield' electrification roadmap—pilot electric sprayers in California have won $90 million in pre-orders—and strategic partnerships like our JV with CNH Industrial for autonomous combines, targeting a 12% margin uplift through 2025.

Quickly, energy and power gen orders were $220 million, up 17% YoY with book-to-bill at 1.18x, driven by LNG turbine demand in Qatar and U.S. grid upgrades. Marine and forestry rounded out at $140 million combined, stable YoY.

North America led at 50% of total orders (up 16% YoY), EMEA at 24% (up 12%), Asia-Pacific at 17% (up 2% YoY), and LatAm at 13% (up 22%). Our book-to-bill remains above 1.1x across all regions, underscoring balanced global exposure.

Looking forward, we expect Q4 order intake of $3.0-3.2 billion, with book-to-bill of 1.17-1.22x, assuming stable commodity prices and no major geopolitical disruptions. Strategically, we're investing $450 million in FY24 capex for battery gigafactory expansions in Decatur and OEM autonomy R&D, aiming to grow adjusted EBITDA margins to 28% by year-end. We've also announced the tuck-in acquisition of a Swedish IoT sensor firm to accelerate our 'Equipment-as-a-Service' model, targeting 15% of revenues by 2026.

Before we open the line for Q&A, I'd like to provide some color on our lead times for key products and components, as this continues to be a focal point for investors given the ongoing supply chain dynamics in the industrial equipment sector. As you know, lead times are a critical leading indicator for our manufacturing throughput, backlog conversion, and ultimately, free cash flow generation. We've made meaningful progress here in Q3, reflecting the resilience of our supply chain initiatives amid persistent headwinds like Red Sea disruptions and lingering semiconductor constraints.

Let me start with the headline numbers. Our weighted average lead time across our core portfolio—encompassing CNC machining centers, hydraulic forging presses, and automated assembly lines—stood at 14.2 weeks at quarter-end, down 18% sequentially from 17.3 weeks in Q2 and 22% year-over-year from 18.2 weeks in Q3 2023. This puts us at the lower end of our peer set; for context, Caterpillar reported averages around 16 weeks for their large earthmoving equipment last quarter, while Siemens noted 15-18 weeks for their industrial automation skids. Our book-to-bill ratio remains healthy at 1.25x, supported by this compression, with our $2.8 billion backlog now 65% weighted toward shorter-lead items under 12 weeks.

Breaking it down by product line, our flagship TitanFlex CNC series—our high-precision 5-axis mills used heavily in aerospace and automotive fab shops—saw lead times drop to 12 weeks from 16 weeks QoQ, thanks to ramped capacity at our new Greenville, South Carolina facility. This is ahead of our internal target of 13 weeks and reflects 92% on-time delivery rates, up from 78% a year ago. For our heavy-duty hydraulic presses, like the 5,000-ton models popular in oil & gas forging, we're at 18 weeks, stable QoQ but down from 24 weeks YoY, as steel casting availability normalized post-Ukraine-related alloy shortages.

On the components side, where we've faced the most volatility, progress has been equally encouraging. Critical-path items like rare earth permanent magnet motors for our servo drives—sourced primarily from Asia—improved to 10 weeks from 14 weeks, driven by dual-sourcing with U.S.-based MP Materials and our new offtake agreement with Lynas Rare Earths in Australia. Semiconductor lead times for our PLC controllers and vision systems, which peaked at 28 weeks during the 2022 chip crunch akin to what NVIDIA and Broadcom endured, are now at 8 weeks, aligning with TSMC's Fab 18 ramp-up in Taiwan. Steel and aluminum forgings averaged 6 weeks, benefiting from U.S. Steel's Big River Steel expansion and our strategic stockpiling, which added 15% to working capital but de-risked 85% of our Q4 builds.

Regionally, we're seeing divergence that underscores our localization strategy. In the Americas, which represent 55% of our bookings, lead times average 12.5 weeks—bolstered by nearshoring to Mexico via our Querétaro plant, where we've localized 70% of stamped components to sidestep Panama Canal delays. EMEA is at 15 weeks, pressured by energy costs but offset by our expanded footprint with thyssenkrupp in Germany for precision gears. APAC, at 16.8 weeks or 25% of mix, remains the laggard due to tariff frictions and Typhoon Gaemi disruptions, but our joint venture with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries in Japan has cut module lead times by 25% for wind turbine nacelles.

These improvements stem from several technical and strategic initiatives we've accelerated. First, our AI-driven demand sensing platform, integrated with SAP S/4HANA and powered by Palantir Foundry, now provides 95% forecast accuracy out to 26 weeks, enabling proactive component pulls—similar to how Rockwell Automation uses predictive analytics for their Logix controllers. We've also invested $150 million in vertical integration, including a new magnet sintering line in Ohio, reducing external dependency from 40% to 28% for electro-mechanical assemblies. Capacity utilization hit 88% in Q3, up from 76% YoY, with digital twin simulations from Siemens NX optimizing our Mexico lines for 20% throughput gains.

Strategically, this positions us well for margin expansion. Shorter lead times have accelerated revenue recognition by $120 million in Q3 versus guidance, boosting segment adjusted EBITDA margins to 24.2% from 21.8%. Looking forward, we expect further compression to 12-13 weeks by year-end through Q4 supplier audits and our 'Resilient Supply 2.0' program, which includes blockchain traceability for 100% of Tier 2 components. This not only mitigates risks from potential U.S.-China trade escalations but also enhances customer stickiness—our Net Promoter Score rose 12 points to 68 amid better delivery predictability.

In summary, lead time compression is a testament to our execution in a volatile macro, directly fueling backlog conversion and ROIC above our 15% hurdle.

Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. I'll now turn to our demand trends across our key end markets—construction, mining, agriculture, and general manufacturing—which continue to drive our top-line performance. Overall, we saw a 7% year-over-year increase in order intake in Q3, with our backlog now standing at a robust $12.4 billion, up 15% from the prior year. This reflects sustained capex momentum from our OEM customers and end-users alike, despite some macro headwinds like elevated interest rates and softening commodity prices in select areas. Let me break this down by end market, with some regional color and our strategic lens.

Starting with construction, which represents about 35% of our revenue mix. Demand remains resilient, fueled by global infrastructure tailwinds. In North America, we're benefiting from the IIJA's ongoing disbursements—over $500 billion in committed spend through 2026—driving excavator and wheel loader shipments up 12% YoY. Housing starts are stabilizing at around 1.4 million annualized units, per Census Bureau data, supporting our mid-sized dozer and telehandler lines. Non-residential remains the star, with data center builds—think hyperscalers like AWS and Google—pushing crane and lift orders 18% higher. In EMEA, UK and EU recovery plans have lifted our asphalt paver backlog by 9%, though German construction PMI at 42 signals some near-term caution. Asia-Pacific is mixed: China's property sector deleveraging caps growth at 3%, but India's $1.4 trillion National Infrastructure Pipeline is accelerating compact track loader demand by 22%. Strategically, we're leaning into our Site Optimization Suite—our telematics platform integrated with Cat Command-like autonomy—to help contractors boost utilization rates from 65% to 75%, which is winning share against Komatsu and Volvo CE.

Moving to mining, our highest-margin segment at 28% of mix. Here, demand is exceptionally strong, with haul truck and drill rig orders up 14% YoY, driven by copper and lithium supercycles tied to electrification. Copper prices hovering at $4.20 per pound underscore the need for larger 400-ton-class trucks like our new MT785AC, with battery-electric pilots converting 20% of our Pilbara fleet orders. Gold miners are holding firm despite AISC pressures, contributing to a 10% rise in our hydraulic shovel bookings. Regionally, Latin America shines—Peru and Chile account for 60% of our APAC/LATAM mining intake, up 25% on Codelco and BHP expansions. Australia faces labor shortages but offsets with autonomous haulage; our Ultra Class solutions have captured 15% market share from Liebherr. North America sees steady gold and potash demand, though we're monitoring Glencore's capex cuts. On initiatives, our e-Powertrain roadmap—aiming for 30% of mining fleet electrified by 2028—includes hydrogen fuel cell retrofits, positioning us ahead of Sandvik's Battery Spot programs.

Agriculture weighs in at 22% of our portfolio, and trends here are bifurcated but positive overall. North American farm incomes, projected at $128 billion by USDA for 2024, are sustaining high-horsepower tractor pulls—our 400+ HP models saw 8% volume growth, aided by Section 179 tax incentives. Precision ag adoption is key: our AutoPath cabin tech, with RTK guidance, boosted aftermarket sensor revenue 25%, mirroring Deere's StarFire ecosystem. In Brazil, soybean acres expanding to 46 million hectares drove planter and sprayer orders up 16%, despite El Niño residuals. Europe faces headwinds—EU nitrogen regulations and Ukraine war spillovers have tempered demand, with tractor registrations down 5% per CEMA data—but our variable-rate fertilizer kits are gaining traction amid subsidy shifts. Asia's rice mechanization wave in India and Indonesia lifted combine harvester shipments 11%. Forward, we're investing $250 million in autonomous orchard platforms, targeting a $5 billion TAM by 2030, to counter labor shortages and compete with AGCO's Fendt agronomy tools.

Finally, general manufacturing, at 15% of mix, is accelerating on reshoring and Industry 4.0. U.S. CHIPS Act and IRA incentives are spurring factory automation—our CNC machining centers and palletizers saw 11% order growth, with utilization rates at OEMs like Tesla and Intel hitting 85%. Supply chain onshoring has revived metalworking demand, up 9% in our lathe and mill lines. EMEA benefits from battery gigafactory builds in Hungary and Germany, while China's EV overcapacity pressures low-end segments but boosts high-precision robotics. Strategically, our Digital Twin Factory platform—leveraging Siemens MindSphere-like IoT—has reduced customer downtime by 20%, driving 30% recurring software revenue growth.

Regionally, North America contributed 48% of Q3 orders, up 10%; EMEA flat at 25% amid energy transition capex; Asia-Pacific up 8% to 20% on selective infrastructure; and LATAM strong at 7%. Looking ahead, we see mid-single-digit demand growth into 2025, with aftermarket—now 42% of revenue—providing insulation via our 98% parts availability SLA. We're allocating $1.2 billion in capex to electrification and autonomy R&D, targeting 15% EBITDA margins by fiscal '26.

Thank you, Mike. Now, turning to our full-year 2024 guidance, we're projecting consolidated revenue of $5.25 billion to $5.45 billion, representing organic growth of 8% to 12% year-over-year, with adjusted EBITDA margins expanding 150 to 250 basis points to 22% to 24%. Free cash flow remains a key focus, targeting $650 million to $750 million, supported by disciplined working capital management and capex of around 4% of sales.

Let me walk you through the key assumptions underpinning this outlook, which are grounded in our rolling 12-month order book—currently at a healthy book-to-bill of 1.15x—current quoting activity, and conversations with our top 100 customers, who represent over 55% of our backlog. We've stress-tested these against downside scenarios, including a potential 50 bps Fed rate cut delay or a sharper-than-expected China slowdown.

First, on the macro front: We're baking in global GDP growth of 3.1%, per our internal blend of IMF and OECD forecasts, with U.S. real GDP at 2.4%, Eurozone at 1.6%, and China at 4.8%. Industrial production trends are equally constructive: U.S. IP up 2.5%, aligned with recent ISM Manufacturing PMI readings hovering in the mid-50s. We assume no broad-based recession, with global capex cycles in our served markets inflecting positively—think OEMs like Caterpillar and John Deere ramping equipment builds post-2023 destocking.

End-market demand is the linchpin here, and we're seeing broad-based recovery with pockets of acceleration. Aerospace & Defense, which is about 25% of our mix, drives the upside: we assume 12% to 15% sector growth, fueled by Boeing's 737 MAX and 787 backlog stabilization and Airbus A320neo ramp-ups. Our precision CNC machining centers and titanium forging presses are perfectly positioned, with order intake up 28% quarter-over-quarter. Automotive, at 20% of sales, we model flat-to-2% growth amid the EV transition—legacy ICE platforms like Ford's F-150 still need our hydraulic forming and robotic welding systems, but we're gaining share in battery gigafactory tooling, targeting 15% penetration by year-end.

Oil & Gas/Marines, roughly 15% of the portfolio, assumes mid-single-digit expansion at 5% to 7%, as upstream capex rebounds to $650 billion globally—ExxonMobil and Chevron's Permian Basin projects will pull through demand for our high-pressure subsea valves and API-compliant drilling rigs. Semiconductors and electronics, now 12% post our Fanuc-partnered robotic arm JV, we expect 10% growth tied to AI data center builds; think TSMC's Arizona fab and Samsung's Texas expansions needing our cleanroom-compatible wafer handling equipment.

Renewables and power gen round out at 18%, with 8% assumed growth: offshore wind farm orders from Ørsted and Vestas for our monopile driving hammers, plus U.S. IRA-driven solar tracker hydraulics. The laggard is general industrials at 10% of mix, flat as reshoring pauses, but our aftermarket services—up 14% YoY—provide a 65% gross margin buffer.

Regionally, North America remains our anchor at 58% of projected sales, growing 9% to 11% on U.S. manufacturing repatriation—CHIPS Act fabs and onshoring from the likes of Intel are filling our Ohio and Texas plants to 92% utilization. EMEA at 22% assumes 6% growth, cautious on German auto weakness (VW and BMW destocking) but offset by UK North Sea revivals and French nuclear SMR investments. Asia-Pacific, 20% of sales, we pencil in 7% to 9%, led by India's capex boom—Reliance and Tata Steel ordering our plate mills—but tempered by China's property drag; we're assuming property-related machinery demand bottoms at -5%, with offsets from EV battery lines.

Strategically, these assumptions embed our execution levers. We're assuming 2 to 3 points of pricing power from steel pass-throughs and value engineering on our IndusTronik platform—our IoT-enabled predictive maintenance suite, now on 40% of new CNC lathes, boosting aftermarket attach rates to 25%. Technical initiatives like our generative AI-optimized nesting software for sheet metal fab cut cycle times 18%, enabling 5% capacity unlock without new capex. Supply chain resilience is key: we assume V-shaped recovery in electronics components, with dual-sourcing from Vietnam and Mexico mitigating any lingering Red Sea disruptions—our inventory turns improved to 5.2x last quarter.

Of course, these are point estimates with risks: a prolonged Middle East conflict could shave 1 to 2 points off Oil & Gas; softer U.S. consumer spending might pressure auto OEMs. Upside comes from share gains—our Q4 pipeline is 20% above plan—and potential M&A bolt-ons in automation, like the rumored Siemens robotics tuck-in.

We're confident in this guidance as it reflects not just cyclical tailwinds but our structural advantages in high-precision, mission-critical equipment.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. To ask a question, press star one. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the demand environment you're seeing in the construction market?

Mike Reynolds (CEO):
Thanks for the question, John. As Lisa detailed earlier, construction demand remains resilient at 35% of our mix, with North American strength from IIJA disbursements driving 12% YoY growth in excavators and wheel loaders. Data centers are a standout, pushing crane orders up 18%, while India's infrastructure pipeline accelerates compact track loaders by 22%. We're countering any EMEA softness with our Site Optimization Suite, boosting utilization and share gains. Overall, we're optimistic on the sector's tailwinds.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Carter with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter (JPMorgan):
What are your expectations for capital expenditures in the coming year?

Lisa Chen (CFO):
Good question, Emily. For FY25, we're guiding capex to about 4.5% of sales, or roughly $1.25 billion, focused on battery gigafactory expansions in Decatur, autonomy R&D, and supply chain localization like our Querétaro plant. This builds on our $450 million FY24 spend, targeting EBITDA margins above 28% and supporting lead time compression to 12 weeks. It aligns with our free cash flow outlook of $700 million midpoint, prioritizing growth and shareholder returns.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Lee (Morgan Stanley):
How are you managing supply chain disruptions, and what impact are they having on your margins?

Mike Reynolds (CEO):
David, thanks. We've made great strides, as Lisa outlined, with average lead times down 22% YoY to 14.2 weeks through dual-sourcing rare earths, AI demand sensing via Palantir, and vertical integration like our Ohio magnet line. Red Sea and chip issues persist, but our Resilient Supply 2.0 program with blockchain traceability has de-risked Q4 builds, accelerating revenue by $120 million and lifting EBITDA margins to 24.2%. Margins are expanding despite disruptions, thanks to 88% capacity utilization and digital twins.

Operator:
Thank you. There are no further questions at this time.

Closing Remarks:

Mike Reynolds (CEO):
Thank you for your questions and your interest in Titan Industrial Equipment. We are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering long-term value for our shareholders.

Sarah Johnson (VP of Investor Relations):
Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call. Have a great day.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
